entries.answer:
Ez egy klasszikus **context overflow** probléma, és a megoldás nem egyetlen technika, hanem egy **rétegzett memóriarendszer** — amely utánozza az emberi memória működését (rövid távú + hosszú távú emlékek). Íme a teljes architektúra, amit a Jaide-hoz érdemes implementálni.

***

## A probléma gyökere

Az LLM kontextus-ablaka olyan, mint a munkamemória: egyszerre csak annyi fér bele, amennyi a limit. Ha a chat hosszabb, a modell egyszerűen nem "látja" a korai üzeneteket. Az 1 millió tokenes ablak sem végtelen — egy elég hosszú chat simán átlépi. A cél nem az, hogy növeljük az ablakot a végtelenbe, hanem hogy **okosan kezeljük, mit tartunk benne**.[1][2]

***

## A megoldás: Hierarchikus Memóriarétegek

A rendszer három szintű memóriát kezel párhuzamosan, és automatikusan dönt arról, melyikből merít.[3]

### 1. réteg – Working Memory (azonnali kontextus)

Ez az aktív kontextusablak — az utolsó \(N\) üzenet, amely 100%-os hűséggel szerepel a promptban. Mérete rugalmas, de általában az összes token ~60–70%-a van fenntartva neki. Ha az ablak elér 70–80%-os telítettséget, automatikusan triggerelődik a következő réteg.[4]

### 2. réteg – Episodic Memory (összefoglalók)

Amikor az első réteg tele lesz, a legrégebbi üzenet-blokkok **nem törlődnek, hanem összefoglalódnak**. Az LLM maga generál egy tömör summát az adott szegmensről, amely tartalmazza a kulcsdöntéseket, neveket, entitásokat és kontextuális tényeket. Ezt a summát egy külső store-ban tároljuk, és minden promptba beillesztjük a working memory elé — sokkal kevesebb tokent foglal, mint az eredeti szöveg.[4]

### 3. réteg – Semantic/Vector Memory (RAG)

A teljes chat-előzményből vektoros embeddinget készítünk, és egy **vektoros adatbázisba** (pl. pgvector, Redis, Weaviate) indexelünk minden egyes üzenetet vagy blokk-szegmenst. Minden új üzenetnél a rendszer **szemantikus keresést** végez: megkeresi a teljes előzményből a jelenlegi kérdéshez leginkább releváns részleteket, és ezeket dinamikusan betölti a promptba. Így a modell "emlékszik" egy 3 hónapos régi részletre is, ha az aktuálisan releváns.[5][6]

***

## A Pipeline működése minden üzenetnél

Amikor egy user üzenetet küld, a rendszer a következő sorrendben állítja össze a promptot:[7][3]

**System prompt** → **Episodic summaries** (összefoglalt múlt) → **RAG-retrieved snippets** (szemantikusan releváns régi részletek) → **Working memory** (legutóbbi \(K\) üzenet teljes hűséggel) → **Aktuális kérdés**

Ez garantálja, hogy a modell sosem lát üres kontextust, és a korlátot soha nem lépi túl, mert a promptot dinamikusan töltjük fel.[8]

***

## Importance Scoring – Mi kerüljön be?

Nem minden üzenet egyformán fontos. Az elmentett szegmensek rangsorolásánál érdemes kombinált pontszámot számítani:[4]

\[
\text{score}(m) = w_1 \cdot \text{recency}(m) + w_2 \cdot \text{relevance}(m, q) + w_3 \cdot \text{entity\_density}(m)
\]

ahol \(q\) az aktuális kérdés, az `entity_density` a neveket, döntéseket, tényeket méri. A legjobb pontszámú szegmensek kerülnek be a kontextusba, nem egyszerűen a legújabbak.

***

## Konkrét Tech Stack

| Réteg | Ajánlott megoldás |
|---|---|
| Working Memory | In-context message queue, token budget alapján vágva |
| Episodic Memory | LLM-alapú summarization, pl. 50 üzenetenként [4] |
| Vector Store | pgvector (Postgres-be integrálva), Redis Vector, vagy Weaviate [4][6] |
| Retrieval | Cosine similarity + BM25 hibrid keresés [6] |
| Orchestration | LangGraph, OpenSearch Agents, vagy custom Zig pipeline (Jaide-hoz) [1] |

***

## StreamingLLM + Attention Sink trükk

Ha architektúra-szinten akarod kezelni (nem csak promptolással), a **StreamingLLM** technika az első néhány tokent ("attention sinks") mindig megőrzi a kontextusban, majd sliding window-t alkalmaz a többire. Ez végtelen hosszúságú streaminghez is stabilan működik anélkül, hogy a modell "megzavarodni" látszana — a korai tokenek horgonyként tartják stabilan a figyelmet.[2][9]

***

## Összefoglalva: miért működik ez?

A rétegzett megközelítés azért robusztus, mert a modell mindig kap: (1) a legfrissebb teljes kontextust, (2) egy tömör összefoglalót a múltból, és (3) a jelenlegi kérdéshez leginkább releváns régi részleteket. A chat soha nem "esik szét" — legfeljebb a nagyon régi, irreleváns részletek kerülnek háttérbe, de bármikor visszahívhatók a vektoros kereséssel.[6][3]

Below is the rewritten, standalone technical build prompt.

## Build Prompt: Hierarchical Multi-Layer Memory and Context Management System for Long-Running Conversational AI

Construct a complete, production-ready hierarchical memory management system that allows a conversational AI to operate over conversations of unbounded length without being constrained by a fixed context window token limit. The system must never truncate, drop, or fail when a conversation exceeds the model's maximum context size; instead, it must dynamically curate what portion of the conversation history is injected into every model call so that continuity and factual recall are preserved indefinitely.

### Step 1: Define the three-tier memory architecture

Design and implement three distinct, concurrently operating memory tiers, each with its own storage backend, update policy, and retrieval interface.

**Tier 1 — Working Memory (immediate context):** Implement an in-memory message queue holding the most recent N conversation turns in full, unmodified fidelity. Allocate approximately 60–70% of the total available token budget to this tier. Implement a token-counting function that tracks the cumulative token size of the queue after every turn using the exact tokenizer of the target model. When the queue's token usage crosses a configurable saturation threshold of 70–80% of its allocated budget, automatically trigger the eviction-and-summarization process described in Tier 2. Implement the eviction logic as a FIFO (first-in-first-out) mechanism operating on entire conversation turns (not partial messages) to avoid breaking semantic units.

**Tier 2 — Episodic Memory (compressed summaries):** When Tier 1 evicts the oldest block of turns (implement eviction in fixed-size blocks, e.g., every 50 messages), generate a compressed summary of that block using a call to the language model itself. The summarization prompt must explicitly instruct the model to preserve: key decisions made, named entities mentioned, factual claims, unresolved action items, and any stated user preferences or constraints. Store each generated summary as a discrete record in a persistent external key-value or document store, tagged with: a unique block ID, the timestamp range it covers, the original turn indices it replaces, and the summary text itself. On every subsequent model call, retrieve and inject all stored episodic summaries in chronological order, positioned before the working memory block in the final prompt. Implement a secondary compression pass: if the total token size of all episodic summaries exceeds a configurable ceiling (e.g., 15% of total token budget), recursively summarize the oldest summaries into a single higher-level meta-summary, replacing multiple entries with one.

**Tier 3 — Semantic Vector Memory (long-term retrieval):** For every message or evicted block, compute a dense vector embedding using an embedding model and store it in a vector database, indexed alongside the raw text, timestamp, turn indices, and any extracted entity metadata. On every new user message, embed the incoming query and perform a similarity search against the entire vector store to retrieve the top-K most semantically relevant historical snippets, regardless of how far back in the conversation they occurred. Implement the retrieval as a hybrid search combining cosine similarity on embeddings with a lexical BM25 score, and combine the two scores using a weighted sum with configurable weights. Deduplicate retrieved snippets against what is already present in Tier 1 and Tier 2 to avoid redundant token usage.

### Step 2: Implement the importance scoring function

Implement a scoring function used to rank candidate memory segments (both for what gets summarized with highest priority and what gets retrieved from the vector store) before injecting them into the prompt. The function must compute:

score(m) = w1 · recency(m) + w2 · relevance(m, q) + w3 · entity_density(m)

where m is a candidate memory segment, q is the current user query, recency(m) is a normalized decay function based on how long ago the segment occurred, relevance(m, q) is the cosine similarity between the embedding of m and the embedding of q, and entity_density(m) is a normalized count of named entities, decisions, and factual assertions detected in m via a lightweight named-entity extraction pass. Make w1, w2, and w3 configurable numeric weights loaded from a configuration file. Sort all candidate segments by this score in descending order and select the top segments until the allocated token sub-budget for that tier is exhausted.

### Step 3: Build the prompt assembly pipeline

Implement a deterministic pipeline function that runs on every incoming user message and assembles the final prompt sent to the model in the following strict order:

1. System prompt (static instructions)
2. Episodic summaries (Tier 2 output, chronological order)
3. RAG-retrieved snippets (Tier 3 output, ranked by importance score)
4. Working memory (Tier 1 output, most recent K turns, full fidelity)
5. Current user query

Implement a hard token budget enforcer that runs after assembly: compute the total token count of the assembled prompt using the exact tokenizer, and if it exceeds the model's maximum context size, progressively trim from Tier 3 first, then Tier 2, then reduce K in Tier 1 last, until the prompt fits within budget. Never trim or omit the system prompt or the current user query under any circumstance.

### Step 4: Implement the storage backends

Build the persistent storage layer with three components: a relational or document database table for conversation turn history and episodic summaries (must support the full CRUD operations, indexed by conversation ID, turn index, and timestamp); a vector database integration supporting insert, similarity search, and delete operations with configurable distance metric (cosine or dot product); and a caching layer for the working memory queue that persists across process restarts so that an interrupted conversation can be resumed without data loss.

### Step 5: Implement the attention-preserving fallback mechanism

As an additional architecture-level safeguard operating independently of the prompt-assembly pipeline described above, implement a sliding-window attention mechanism at the model inference layer: permanently pin the first M tokens of the original conversation (treated as fixed "attention anchor" tokens) in every inference call regardless of how much later content is added, and apply a sliding window to all tokens after that anchor so that only the most recent window plus the anchor are passed to the model's attention computation. Implement this as a configurable inference-time wrapper that intercepts the token stream before it reaches the model, splices in the anchor tokens, and manages the rolling window boundary as new tokens arrive, ensuring the total token count passed to the model never exceeds its hard maximum context size.

### Step 6: Implement triggers, monitoring, and configuration

Build a monitoring subsystem that logs, for every model call: current token usage per tier, saturation percentage of the working memory, number of episodic summaries currently stored, number of vector retrieval hits and their similarity scores, and total end-to-end latency added by the memory pipeline. Expose all thresholds, weights, token budgets, and window sizes as external configuration parameters that can be changed without modifying source code.

### Deliverable requirements

Deliver the complete, unabridged, fully functional source code for every component described above: the working memory queue manager, the summarization trigger and summarizer module, the vector embedding and hybrid retrieval module, the importance scoring module, the prompt assembly pipeline with budget enforcement, the persistent storage layer with full database schema definitions, the sliding-window attention wrapper, and the monitoring/configuration subsystem. Every file must be complete, syntactically correct, and immediately runnable in a production environment. Do not include placeholders, stub functions, mock data, simulated responses, truncated code sections, or comments indicating incomplete implementation. Every function must contain its full, real logic. Include the complete database schema (tables, indexes, foreign keys), the complete configuration file with all default values populated, and the complete dependency/build manifest required to run the system end to end.
